Mathematical details

mathematical-details.Rmd

This vignette defines the smooth, mean-based estimators in teffects and gives the influence function used for their robust standard errors. The estimators are ordinary regression adjustment (RA), normalized inverse- probability weighting (IPW), inverse-probability-weighted regression adjustment (IPWRA), augmented IPW (AIPW), and the post-lasso AIPW estimator in telasso().

Matching estimators are excluded because their asymptotic theory is different. The final section covers qte(). It estimates quantiles, so inversion of an estimated distribution function replaces the smooth sample-mean calculation and the package uses bootstrap inference. The experimental LATE estimators are not part of the exported API and require an additional instrument, so they are outside the (Xi,Di,Yi)(X_i,D_i,Y_i) setup used here.

Data, identification, and targets

Let the observations

Oi=(Xi,Di,Yi),i=1,…,n, O_i=(X_i,D_i,Y_i), \qquad i=1,\ldots,n,

be independent and identically distributed. Treatment takes values in 𝒦={0,1,…,K−1}\mathcal K=\{0,1,\ldots,K-1\}, with 0 denoting the reference level, and Yi(k)Y_i(k) is the potential outcome under level kk. Define

mk(Xi)=E(Yi∣Di=k,Xi),πk(Xi)=P(Di=k∣Xi). m_k(X_i)=E(Y_i\mid D_i=k,X_i), \qquad \pi_k(X_i)=P(D_i=k\mid X_i).

We write 1(⋅)1(\cdot) for the indicator function.

For a binary treatment, the notation reduces to

π(Xi)=P(Di=1∣Xi),π1(Xi)=π(Xi),π0(Xi)=1−π(Xi). \pi(X_i)=P(D_i=1\mid X_i), \qquad \pi_1(X_i)=\pi(X_i), \qquad \pi_0(X_i)=1-\pi(X_i).

The causal interpretation uses the usual conditions:

Yi=Yi(Di),Yi(k)⟂⟂Di∣Xi,0<πk(Xi)<1 Y_i=Y_i(D_i), \qquad Y_i(k)\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}D_i\mid X_i, \qquad 0<\pi_k(X_i)<1

almost surely for each relevant treatment level. Consistency and conditional exchangeability identify

E{Yi(k)∣Xi}=mk(Xi). E\{Y_i(k)\mid X_i\}=m_k(X_i).

Use one notation for population, treated, and control targets. Let t=⋆t=\star denote the full population and let t=g∈𝒦t=g\in\mathcal K denote the population receiving treatment gg. Set

a⋆i=1,r⋆(Xi)=1,q⋆=1,agi=1(Di=g),rg(Xi)=πg(Xi),qg=P(Di=g). \begin{aligned} a_{\star i}&=1, & r_\star(X_i)&=1, & q_\star&=1,\\ a_{gi}&=1(D_i=g), & r_g(X_i)&=\pi_g(X_i), & q_g&=P(D_i=g). \end{aligned}

The potential-outcome mean in target population tt is

θk∣t=E{atiYi(k)}qt=E{atimk(Xi)}qt. \theta_{k\mid t} = \frac{E\{a_{ti}Y_i(k)\}}{q_t} = \frac{E\{a_{ti}m_k(X_i)\}}{q_t}.

Thus θk∣⋆=E{Yi(k)}\theta_{k\mid\star}=E\{Y_i(k)\}. For a focal level k≠0k\ne0,

ATE⁡k,0=θk∣⋆−θ0∣⋆,ATT⁡k,0=θk∣k−θ0∣k,ATC⁡k,0=θk∣0−θ0∣0. \begin{aligned} \operatorname{ATE}_{k,0} &=\theta_{k\mid\star}-\theta_{0\mid\star},\\ \operatorname{ATT}_{k,0} &=\theta_{k\mid k}-\theta_{0\mid k},\\ \operatorname{ATC}_{k,0} &=\theta_{k\mid 0}-\theta_{0\mid 0}. \end{aligned}

The transport weight for outcome level kk and target tt is

wk∣t(Oi)=1(Di=k)rt(Xi)πk(Xi). w_{k\mid t}(O_i) = 1(D_i=k)\frac{r_t(X_i)}{\pi_k(X_i)}.

For the full population this is the usual inverse-probability weight 1(Di=k)/πk(Xi)1(D_i=k)/\pi_k(X_i). For target group gg, it is 1(Di=k)πg(Xi)/πk(Xi)1(D_i=k)\pi_g(X_i)/\pi_k(X_i). Notice that wg∣g=1(Di=g)w_{g\mid g}=1(D_i=g) and, when the propensity score is correct, E{wk∣t(Oi)}=qtE\{w_{k\mid t}(O_i)\}=q_t.

Throughout, 𝔼n[f]=n−1∑if(Oi)\mathbb{E}_n[f]=n^{-1}\sum_i f(O_i) denotes the sample average. Hats denote estimates and all population quantities in an influence function are evaluated at the probability limits of the fitted working models. If a working model is misspecified, the formula describes inference around the estimator’s probability limit. It describes inference for the causal target whenever the estimator’s stated consistency condition holds.

Influence-function convention

For a scalar estimand θ\theta, teffects uses the normalization

n(θ̂−θ)=1n∑i=1nϕi+op(1),E(ϕi)=0. \sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_i+o_p(1), \qquad E(\phi_i)=0.

For a vector of estimates, ϕi\phi_i is a row vector. The package stores the sample analogues as fit$influence and computes

Var̂(θ̂)=1n2∑i=1nϕ̂iϕ̂i⊤. \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\theta) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat\phi_i\widehat\phi_i^\top.

This is the variance of θ̂\widehat\theta, not the asymptotic variance of nθ̂\sqrt n\widehat\theta.

Estimated nuisance parameters

We assume the outcome-model covariate vector XiX_i includes an intercept. The implemented outcome model is

mk(Xi;βk)=Xi⊤βk. m_k(X_i;\beta_k)=X_i^\top\beta_k.

Ordinary arm-specific least squares solves

𝔼n[1(Di=k)Xi{Yi−Xi⊤β̂k}]=0. \mathbb{E}_n\left[1(D_i=k)X_i \{Y_i-X_i^\top\widehat\beta_k\}\right]=0.

Writing

Ak=E(1(Di=k)XiXi⊤), A_k=E(1(D_i=k)X_iX_i^\top),

the coefficient influence function is

ϕβk,i=Ak−11(Di=k)Xi{Yi−mk(Xi)}. \phi_{\beta_k,i} = A_k^{-1}1(D_i=k)X_i\{Y_i-m_k(X_i)\}. \tag{1}

Let γ\gamma collect the parameters of the propensity-score equations, including every arm-specific block when necessary. If

𝔼n[sπ(Oi;γ̂)]=0,Jγ=E{∂sπ(Oi;γ)∂γ⊤}, \mathbb{E}_n[s_{\pi}(O_i;\widehat\gamma)]=0, \qquad J_\gamma = E\left\{\frac{\partial s_{\pi}(O_i;\gamma)} {\partial\gamma^\top}\right\},

then

ϕγ,i=−Jγ−1sπ(Oi;γ). \phi_{\gamma,i}=-J_\gamma^{-1}s_{\pi}(O_i;\gamma). \tag{2}

It is convenient to define the log-probability derivative

ℓk(Xi)=∂log⁡πk(Xi;γ)∂γ,ℓ⋆(Xi)=0. \ell_k(X_i) = \frac{\partial\log\pi_k(X_i;\gamma)}{\partial\gamma}, \qquad \ell_\star(X_i)=0.

For a treatment-defined target, ℓt=ℓg\ell_t=\ell_g. It follows that

∂wk∣t(Oi;γ)∂γ=wk∣t(Oi;γ){ℓt(Xi)−ℓk(Xi)}. \frac{\partial w_{k\mid t}(O_i;\gamma)}{\partial\gamma} = w_{k\mid t}(O_i;\gamma) \{\ell_t(X_i)-\ell_k(X_i)\}. \tag{3}

Equations (1)–(3) make the effect of nuisance estimation explicit. Treating π̂k\widehat\pi_k or $\widehatm_k$ as fixed generally omits terms that are present in the package’s robust variance estimator.

Regression adjustment

Definition

Ordinary RA, implemented by ra(), fits

$$ \widehat\beta_k^{RA} = \arg\min_b\sum_{i=1}^n 1(D_i=k)(Y_i-X_i^\top b)^2, \qquad \widehatm_k(X_i)=X_i^\top\widehat\beta_k^{RA}. $$

It then standardizes predictions to the observed target population:

$$ \widehat\theta_{k\mid t}^{RA} = \frac{\mathbb{E}_n[a_{ti}\widehatm_k(X_i)]} {\mathbb{E}_n[a_{ti}]}. \tag{4} $$

For t=⋆t=\star, equation (4) averages over the full sample. For an ATT or ATC, it averages over the observations in the corresponding treatment group.

Influence function

Define the target-population regressor mean

bt=E(atiXi)qt. b_t=\frac{E(a_{ti}X_i)}{q_t}.

The RA influence function for θk∣t\theta_{k\mid t} is

ϕk∣t,iRA=atiqt{mk(Xi)−θk∣t}+bt⊤ϕβk,i. \boxed{ \phi_{k\mid t,i}^{RA} = \frac{a_{ti}}{q_t} \{m_k(X_i)-\theta_{k\mid t}\} +b_t^\top\phi_{\beta_k,i}. } \tag{5}

The first term captures sampling variation in the covariate distribution used for standardization. The second propagates estimation of the arm-specific outcome regression. RA is consistent for the causal target when the corresponding conditional outcome model is correctly specified.

Propensity-score estimating equations

All propensity-score methods enter the influence functions below through ϕγ,i\phi_{\gamma,i} in (2). We also write XiX_i for the treatment-model covariate vector. The exact score sπs_\pi depends on psmethod.

For binary maximum-likelihood logit or probit, write π(Xi;γ)=G(Xi⊤γ)\pi(X_i;\gamma)=G(X_i^\top\gamma) and gi=G′(Xi⊤γ)g_i=G'(X_i^\top\gamma). The score is

sπ(Oi;γ)=Xi{Di−π(Xi;γ)}giπ(Xi;γ){1−π(Xi;γ)}. s_{\pi}(O_i;\gamma) = X_i \frac{\{D_i-\pi(X_i;\gamma)\}g_i} {\pi(X_i;\gamma)\{1-\pi(X_i;\gamma)\}}. \tag{6}

For logit, this simplifies to Xi{Di−π(Xi;γ)}X_i\{D_i-\pi(X_i;\gamma)\}. A multivalued treatment uses the usual multinomial-logit score.

Inverse-probability tilting (IPT) uses a logistic tilt. For an ATE or potential-outcome mean, it fits one arm-specific score from

𝔼n[Xi{1(Di=k)πk(Xi;γk)−1}]=0 \mathbb{E}_n\left[ X_i\left\{\frac{1(D_i=k)}{\pi_k(X_i;\gamma_k)}-1\right\} \right]=0 \tag{7}

for every kk. With an intercept, (7) makes the arm’s raw inverse- probability weights sum to nn. For a binary ATT, the same equation is fit for the comparison arm k=0k=0; for a binary ATC it is fit for k=1k=1. The arm-specific binary IPT fits used for ATEs need not add to one, but each π̂k(Xi)\widehat\pi_k(X_i) enters the estimator and its influence function in the same way as a generalized propensity score.

For binary covariate-balancing propensity scores (CBPS), the implemented equations are

ATE or POM:𝔼n[XiDi−π(Xi)π(Xi){1−π(Xi)}]=0,ATT:𝔼n[XiDi−π(Xi)1−π(Xi)]=0,ATC:𝔼n[XiDi−π(Xi)π(Xi)]=0. \begin{array}{ll} \text{ATE or POM:}& \mathbb{E}_n\left[X_i\dfrac{D_i-\pi(X_i)} {\pi(X_i)\{1-\pi(X_i)\}}\right]=0,\\[10pt] \text{ATT:}& \mathbb{E}_n\left[X_i\dfrac{D_i-\pi(X_i)}{1-\pi(X_i)}\right]=0,\\[10pt] \text{ATC:}& \mathbb{E}_n\left[X_i\dfrac{D_i-\pi(X_i)}{\pi(X_i)}\right]=0. \end{array} \tag{8}

For a multivalued treatment, the CBPS implementation balances adjacent arms:

𝔼n[Xi{1(Di=k)πk(Xi)−1(Di=k−1)πk−1(Xi)}]=0,k=1,…,K−1. \mathbb{E}_n\left[ X_i\left\{ \frac{1(D_i=k)}{\pi_k(X_i)} - \frac{1(D_i=k-1)}{\pi_{k-1}(X_i)} \right\} \right]=0, \qquad k=1,\ldots,K-1. \tag{9}

The Jacobian of the selected equations supplies JγJ_\gamma in (2).

Normalized inverse-probability weighting

Definition

For every outcome level and target population, ipw() uses the normalized, or Hájek, estimator

θ̂k∣tIPW=𝔼n[ŵk∣t(Oi)Yi]𝔼n[ŵk∣t(Oi)]. \widehat\theta_{k\mid t}^{IPW} = \frac{\mathbb{E}_n[\widehat w_{k\mid t}(O_i)Y_i]} {\mathbb{E}_n[\widehat w_{k\mid t}(O_i)]}. \tag{10}

For an ATE, these are normalized inverse-probability-weighted arm means. For an ATT or ATC, equation (10) uses normalized odds weights to transport outcomes from arm kk to the target arm.

Influence function

Let

Hk∣t=E{wk∣t(Oi)} H_{k\mid t}=E\{w_{k\mid t}(O_i)\}

and define the propensity loading

ck∣tIPW=1Hk∣tE[wk∣t(Oi){Yi−θk∣t}{ℓt(Xi)−ℓk(Xi)}]. c_{k\mid t}^{IPW} = \frac{1}{H_{k\mid t}} E\left[ w_{k\mid t}(O_i) \{Y_i-\theta_{k\mid t}\} \{\ell_t(X_i)-\ell_k(X_i)\} \right].

The influence function is

ϕk∣t,iIPW=wk∣t(Oi)Hk∣t{Yi−θk∣t}+(ck∣tIPW)⊤ϕγ,i. \boxed{ \phi_{k\mid t,i}^{IPW} = \frac{w_{k\mid t}(O_i)}{H_{k\mid t}} \{Y_i-\theta_{k\mid t}\} + \left(c_{k\mid t}^{IPW}\right)^\top\phi_{\gamma,i}. } \tag{11}

The first term is the influence function if the propensity score were known. The second captures estimation of the propensity score and is included by teffects. If the propensity model is correct, Hk∣t=qtH_{k\mid t}=q_t. If k=t=gk=t=g, the weight is simply 1(Di=g)1(D_i=g), its derivative is zero, and (11) reduces to the influence function of the observed mean in group gg.

Normalized IPW is consistent for the causal target when the propensity-score model is correctly specified.

Inverse-probability-weighted regression adjustment

Definition

ipwra() implements IPWRA. For each outcome level and target, it solves the weighted least-squares problem

β̂k∣tIPWRA=arg⁡minb∑i=1nŵk∣t(Oi)(Yi−Xi⊤b)2. \widehat\beta_{k\mid t}^{IPWRA} = \arg\min_b\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat w_{k\mid t}(O_i)(Y_i-X_i^\top b)^2. \tag{12}

The fitted regression is then standardized over the observed target group:

θ̂k∣tIPWRA=𝔼n[atiXi⊤β̂k∣tIPWRA]𝔼n[ati]. \widehat\theta_{k\mid t}^{IPWRA} = \frac{\mathbb{E}_n[a_{ti}X_i^\top \widehat\beta_{k\mid t}^{IPWRA}]} {\mathbb{E}_n[a_{ti}]}. \tag{13}

For a binary ATT, for example, the treated regression has unit weights and the control regression has odds weights π(Xi)/{1−π(Xi)}\pi(X_i)/\{1-\pi(X_i)\}. With a multivalued treatment, the package fits a separate pair of transported regressions for each focal ATT or ATC contrast.

Influence function

For brevity, write mk(Xi)=Xi⊤βk∣tm_k(X_i)=X_i^\top\beta_{k\mid t} in this section and define

Ak∣tw=E{wk∣t(Oi)XiXi⊤},Ck∣t=E[wk∣t(Oi)Xi{Yi−mk(Xi)}{ℓt(Xi)−ℓk(Xi)}⊤]. \begin{aligned} A_{k\mid t}^{w} &=E\{w_{k\mid t}(O_i)X_iX_i^\top\},\\ C_{k\mid t} &=E\left[ w_{k\mid t}(O_i)X_i \{Y_i-m_k(X_i)\} \{\ell_t(X_i)-\ell_k(X_i)\}^\top \right]. \end{aligned}

The weighted-regression coefficient influence function is

ϕβk∣t,iw=(Ak∣tw)−1[wk∣t(Oi)Xi{Yi−mk(Xi)}+Ck∣tϕγ,i]. \phi_{\beta_{k\mid t},i}^{w} = \left(A_{k\mid t}^{w}\right)^{-1} \left[ w_{k\mid t}(O_i)X_i\{Y_i-m_k(X_i)\} +C_{k\mid t}\phi_{\gamma,i} \right]. \tag{14}

Consequently,

ϕk∣t,iIPWRA=atiqt{mk(Xi)−θk∣t}+bt⊤ϕβk∣t,iw. \boxed{ \phi_{k\mid t,i}^{IPWRA} = \frac{a_{ti}}{q_t} \{m_k(X_i)-\theta_{k\mid t}\} +b_t^\top\phi_{\beta_{k\mid t},i}^{w}. } \tag{15}

The Ck∣tϕγ,iC_{k\mid t}\phi_{\gamma,i} term propagates estimation of the propensity score through the weighted regression. It disappears if the propensity score is treated as known or if the outcome regression is correct, because then the relevant weighted residual expectation is zero.

With an intercept and the required regularity conditions, IPWRA is doubly robust: (13) is consistent when either the linear outcome model or the propensity-score model is correctly specified.

Augmented inverse-probability weighting

Definition

aipw() first fits the unweighted arm-specific outcome regressions used by RA. It then defines

$$ \widehat h_{k\mid t,i} = a_{ti}\widehatm_k(X_i) + \widehat w_{k\mid t}(O_i) \{Y_i-\widehatm_k(X_i)\} $$

and estimates

θ̂k∣tAIPW=𝔼n[ĥk∣t,i]𝔼n[ati]. \widehat\theta_{k\mid t}^{AIPW} = \frac{\mathbb{E}_n[\widehat h_{k\mid t,i}]}{\mathbb{E}_n[a_{ti}]}. \tag{16}

For the full population, (16) is the familiar average of

$$ \widehatm_k(X_i) + \frac{1(D_i=k)}{\widehat\pi_k(X_i)} \{Y_i-\widehatm_k(X_i)\}. $$

For a binary ATT, the counterfactual control mean is

$$ \widehat\theta_{0\mid1}^{AIPW} = \frac{1}{\sum_iD_i} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ D_i\widehatm_0(X_i) +(1-D_i)\frac{\widehat\pi(X_i)}{1-\widehat\pi(X_i)} \{Y_i-\widehatm_0(X_i)\} \right]. $$

Influence function

Define the two nuisance loadings

cβ,k∣tAIPW=1qtE[{ati−wk∣t(Oi)}Xi],cγ,k∣tAIPW=1qtE[wk∣t(Oi){Yi−mk(Xi)}{ℓt(Xi)−ℓk(Xi)}]. \begin{aligned} c_{\beta,k\mid t}^{AIPW} &= \frac{1}{q_t}E[\{a_{ti}-w_{k\mid t}(O_i)\}X_i],\\ c_{\gamma,k\mid t}^{AIPW} &= \frac{1}{q_t}E\left[ w_{k\mid t}(O_i)\{Y_i-m_k(X_i)\} \{\ell_t(X_i)-\ell_k(X_i)\} \right]. \end{aligned}

The influence function implemented by the parametric AIPW estimator is

ϕk∣t,iAIPW=1qt[ati{mk(Xi)−θk∣t}+wk∣t(Oi){Yi−mk(Xi)}]+(cβ,k∣tAIPW)⊤ϕβk,i+(cγ,k∣tAIPW)⊤ϕγ,i. \boxed{ \begin{aligned} \phi_{k\mid t,i}^{AIPW} ={}& \frac{1}{q_t} \left[ a_{ti}\{m_k(X_i)-\theta_{k\mid t}\} +w_{k\mid t}(O_i)\{Y_i-m_k(X_i)\} \right]\\ &+ \left(c_{\beta,k\mid t}^{AIPW}\right)^\top \phi_{\beta_k,i} + \left(c_{\gamma,k\mid t}^{AIPW}\right)^\top \phi_{\gamma,i}. \end{aligned} } \tag{17}

If both nuisance models are correct, both loadings are zero. Equation (17) then reduces to the efficient influence function

ϕk∣t,ieff=1qt[ati{mk(Xi)−θk∣t}+wk∣t(Oi){Yi−mk(Xi)}]. \boxed{ \phi_{k\mid t,i}^{eff} = \frac{1}{q_t} \left[ a_{ti}\{m_k(X_i)-\theta_{k\mid t}\} +w_{k\mid t}(O_i)\{Y_i-m_k(X_i)\} \right]. } \tag{18}

If exactly one working model is correct, (16) remains consistent but one of the chain-rule corrections in (17) can remain nonzero. This is why the parametric implementation uses the complete expression (17), rather than always treating (18) as the influence function.

Post-lasso and cross-fitted AIPW

telasso() is a binary-treatment implementation of the same AIPW functional in (16). It uses plugin lasso to select outcome regressors separately in each arm and to select propensity-score regressors, then refits the selected models without a penalty.

With LL cross-fitting folds, let ℓ(i)\ell(i) be observation ii’s fold and let $\widehatm_k^{(-\ell(i))}$ and π̂(−ℓ(i))\widehat\pi^{(-\ell(i))} be trained without that fold. Substituting these out-of-fold predictions into (16) defines the cross-fitted estimate. If multiple random partitions are requested, telasso() averages the estimates from the partitions.

Under overlap, suitable moment conditions, approximate sparsity, and nuisance rates satisfying the usual product-rate condition, Neyman orthogonality makes first-order nuisance-estimation terms disappear. Its influence function is therefore (18). In binary notation, the full-population versions are

ϕ1∣⋆,itelasso=m1(Xi)−θ1∣⋆+Diπ(Xi){Yi−m1(Xi)},ϕ0∣⋆,itelasso=m0(Xi)−θ0∣⋆+1−Di1−π(Xi){Yi−m0(Xi)}. \begin{aligned} \phi_{1\mid\star,i}^{telasso} &= m_1(X_i)-\theta_{1\mid\star} +\frac{D_i}{\pi(X_i)}\{Y_i-m_1(X_i)\},\\ \phi_{0\mid\star,i}^{telasso} &= m_0(X_i)-\theta_{0\mid\star} +\frac{1-D_i}{1-\pi(X_i)}\{Y_i-m_0(X_i)\}. \end{aligned} \tag{19}

The stored influence values are the estimated orthogonal scores, averaged over repeated partitions. No finite-dimensional post-selection chain-rule term is added. With xfolds = 1, the same score is evaluated using full-sample nuisance fits; its validity therefore requires stronger conditions than the cross-fitted construction.

Contrasts and reported coefficients

Every mean-based estimator first obtains influence functions for the relevant potential-outcome means. Linear contrasts require no new derivation. If

τ̂k,0∣t=θ̂k∣t−θ̂0∣t, \widehat\tau_{k,0\mid t} = \widehat\theta_{k\mid t}-\widehat\theta_{0\mid t},

then, for any estimator EE,

ϕτk,0∣t,iE=ϕk∣t,iE−ϕ0∣t,iE. \boxed{ \phi_{\tau_{k,0\mid t},i}^{E} = \phi_{k\mid t,i}^{E}-\phi_{0\mid t,i}^{E}. } \tag{20}

The efficient influence functions for the binary treatment-effect targets follow directly from (18). Write p1=P(Di=1)p_1=P(D_i=1), p0=P(Di=0)p_0=P(D_i=0), and suppress the observation subscript on the right-hand sides. Then

ϕATEeff=m1(X)−m0(X)−ATE⁡+Dπ(X){Y−m1(X)}−1−D1−π(X){Y−m0(X)},ϕATTeff=1p1[D{Y−m0(X)−ATT}−(1−D)π(X)1−π(X){Y−m0(X)}],ϕATCeff=1p0[(1−D){m1(X)−Y−ATC}+D1−π(X)π(X){Y−m1(X)}]. \begin{aligned} \phi_{ATE}^{eff} ={}& m_1(X)-m_0(X)-\operatorname{ATE} +\frac{D}{\pi(X)}\{Y-m_1(X)\} -\frac{1-D}{1-\pi(X)}\{Y-m_0(X)\},\\[4pt] \phi_{ATT}^{eff} ={}& \frac{1}{p_1}\left[ D\{Y-m_0(X)-\operatorname{ATT}\} -(1-D)\frac{\pi(X)}{1-\pi(X)}\{Y-m_0(X)\} \right],\\[4pt] \phi_{ATC}^{eff} ={}& \frac{1}{p_0}\left[ (1-D)\{m_1(X)-Y-\operatorname{ATC}\} +D\frac{1-\pi(X)}{\pi(X)}\{Y-m_1(X)\} \right]. \end{aligned} \tag{21}

stat = "pomeans" reports the full-population θk∣⋆\theta_{k\mid\star}. stat = "ate" reports (20) with t=⋆t=\star, stat = "att" uses t=kt=k, and stat = "atc" uses t=0t=0. The additional reference potential-outcome mean printed with a treatment-effect contrast uses the same target population and its corresponding influence-function column.

The following table summarizes the causal consistency condition and the influence function stored by the package.

Estimator Sufficient working-model condition Stored influence function
RA mk(X)m_k(X) correct Equation (5)
normalized IPW πk(X)\pi_k(X) correct Equation (11)
IPWRA mk(X)m_k(X) or πk(X)\pi_k(X) correct Equation (15)
parametric AIPW mk(X)m_k(X) or πk(X)\pi_k(X) correct Equation (17)
telasso() orthogonal-score nuisance-rate conditions Equation (18)

All formulas assume nonsingular population Jacobians, finite second moments, and a fixed estimation population. The default strict-overlap behavior of the package fits this regular setting. Clamping introduces a kink at the clamp boundary, while trimming changes the retained population; inference after either operation should be interpreted with those qualifications.

References

Cattaneo, M. D. (2010). Efficient semiparametric estimation of multivalued treatment effects under ignorability. Journal of Econometrics 155(2), 138–154.

Chernozhukov, V., D. Chetverikov, M. Demirer, E. Duflo, C. Hansen, W. Newey, and J. Robins (2018). Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters. The Econometrics Journal 21(1), C1–C68.
